## Graduate a Gemini Prototype from AI Studio to Vertex AI (`ai-studio-to-vertex`)

Move a Gemini app from an AI Studio API key to Vertex AI with IAM, Application Default Credentials and a least-privilege runtime service account, with no code rewrite.

**Use it when**

- You prototyped with a Gemini API key from Google AI Studio and now need IAM-based access, data governance, VPC/region controls or Google Cloud billing and quotas.
- Your code already uses the google-genai SDK (Python, JS, Go or Java), so switching is a configuration change, not a rewrite.
- You want to stop shipping or storing API keys and use Application Default Credentials locally and a service account in production.

**Do not use it when**

- A hobby or early prototype that is happy on the Gemini API free tier: stay on AI Studio; Vertex AI has no free model quota.
- You need a feature that is only in the Gemini Developer API (check the feature comparison in the docs) before moving.
- You also need to host an agent with tools: use the gemini-adk-service blueprint, which includes this setup plus Cloud Run.
- Your app runs outside Google Cloud and cannot use a service account safely: consider Workload Identity Federation before creating any key files (never download service-account keys for this).

**Cost:** Vertex AI bills Gemini per input and output token, by model, with no free model quota, and needs a billing account. Enabling the API and creating the service account cost nothing by themselves. Compare the official Vertex AI generative AI pricing page with Gemini API pricing and set a budget alert before switching traffic.

**Verified:** syntax-checked on 2026-11-19 (gcloud 594.0.0, python 3.13.5). Maintainer: @rjohnn1

Try it: `doogle explain ai-studio-to-vertex` then `doogle plan ai-studio-to-vertex`

## Gemini ADK Agent Service on Cloud Run + Vertex AI (`gemini-adk-service`)

Deploy an Agent Development Kit (ADK) agent backed by Gemini on Vertex AI as a private Cloud Run service with its own least-privilege identity.

**Use it when**

- You are building an AI agent (tools, multi-step reasoning, sub-agents) with Google ADK and need it hosted as an API.
- You want Gemini via Vertex AI with IAM-based auth (no API keys in code) and per-project quotas and logging.
- The agent should be private by default and called by your own backend, scheduler, or authenticated users.

**Do not use it when**

- You only need a single prompt-and-response call: call the Gemini API directly from your app with the google-genai SDK; no agent framework or server needed.
- You are still experimenting with prompts: prototype in Google AI Studio first, then export code.
- You want a fully managed agent runtime with sessions and memory handled for you: evaluate Vertex AI Agent Engine (deploy with 'adk deploy agent_engine').
- You need a no-code chat agent over your documents: consider Vertex AI Search / Agent Builder style products before writing code.

**Cost:** Gemini on Vertex AI is billed per input and output token and varies a lot by model; agents that loop or call tools can use many tokens per request. Cloud Run, Cloud Build and Artifact Registry have free tiers and then bill by usage. There is no free model quota on Vertex AI, so set a billing budget alert and check the official Vertex AI generative AI pricing page.

**Verified:** syntax-checked on 2026-11-19 (gcloud 594.0.0, python 3.13.5). Maintainer: @rjohnn1

Try it: `doogle explain gemini-adk-service` then `doogle plan gemini-adk-service`

## Solo Serverless API on Cloud Run (`solo-serverless-api`)

Ship a containerised HTTP API from source to Cloud Run with scale-to-zero, no Dockerfile required.

**Use it when**

- You have a small HTTP API or backend (any language with a buildpack or a Dockerfile) and traffic is low or spiky.
- You want pay-per-use with scale-to-zero instead of an always-on VM.
- A side project, prototype, or internal tool that needs a public HTTPS URL quickly.

**Do not use it when**

- Your site is static (HTML/JS only): Firebase Hosting is simpler and cheaper.
- You only need a few event handlers on Firebase data: Cloud Functions for Firebase is less to manage.
- You need sub-100ms cold starts on every request: scale-to-zero adds cold starts; keep min instances above 0 and accept the always-on cost.
- You need long-lived WebSocket-heavy or stateful workloads: consider GKE Autopilot or a Compute Engine VM.
- The API is for internal use only: drop --allow-unauthenticated and use IAM (see GUIDE.md).

**Cost:** Cloud Run, Cloud Build and Artifact Registry each have a free tier that typically covers a low-traffic side project; usage beyond it is billed per request, CPU and memory time, build minutes and stored image size. A billing account must be linked to the project. Check the official Cloud Run pricing page and set a budget alert before going public.

**Verified:** syntax-checked on 2026-11-19 (gcloud 594.0.0, python 3.13.5). Maintainer: @rjohnn1

Try it: `doogle explain solo-serverless-api` then `doogle plan solo-serverless-api`

## Firebase Auth MVP (Hosting + Authentication + Firestore) (`firebase-auth-mvp`)

Launch a small web MVP with sign-in, a Firestore database locked down by security rules, and global static hosting on a free web.app domain.

**Use it when**

- You are building a small web app (plain JS, React, Vue, Svelte...) that needs user sign-in and a database, and you want no servers to run.
- An MVP or hackathon project where the free tier is likely enough and you want a real HTTPS URL today.
- Per-user data that Firestore security rules can protect (each user reads and writes only their own documents).

**Do not use it when**

- A static site with no users or data: Firebase Hosting alone (skip Auth and Firestore) is simpler.
- Heavy relational data, joins, or reporting: Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL) behind a Cloud Run API fits better than Firestore.
- Server-side rendering or a full-stack framework (Next.js, Angular SSR): use Firebase App Hosting instead of classic Hosting.
- Enterprise SSO, SAML, multi-tenancy or SLAs on sign-in: upgrade to Identity Platform and plan for its pricing.
- You need secret server logic (payments, admin actions): add Cloud Functions or a Cloud Run API; never trust the browser.

**Cost:** Hosting, Authentication and Firestore all have no-cost quotas on the Spark plan that usually cover an MVP; usage beyond them (storage, transfer, document reads and writes, some sign-in methods such as phone/SMS) needs the pay-as-you-go Blaze plan. Check the official Firebase pricing page and set a budget alert before launch.

**Verified:** syntax-checked on 2026-11-19 (firebase-tools 15.37.0, gcloud 594.0.0, python 3.13.5). Maintainer: @rjohnn1

Try it: `doogle explain firebase-auth-mvp` then `doogle plan firebase-auth-mvp`

## Google Sheet + Apps Script Webhook (`workspace-sheet-webhook`)

Turn a new Google Sheet into a webhook receiver with a container-bound Apps Script web app, managed from your terminal with clasp.

**Use it when**

- You want form submissions, payment notifications, or IoT pings written straight into a spreadsheet your team already uses.
- Low volume automation (a few requests per minute) where a Sheet is the database and UI.
- You want to keep code in git and deploy Apps Script from the terminal instead of the browser editor.

**Do not use it when**

- You only need to collect form answers: Google Forms already writes responses to a Sheet with zero code.
- You need high throughput, strict latency, or concurrent writes: Apps Script has quotas and execution limits; use Cloud Run plus Firestore or BigQuery instead.
- Sensitive data or authenticated callers: an 'Anyone' web app URL is public; add a shared-secret check (GUIDE.md) or use a Cloud Run service with IAM.
- You need workflows across many SaaS tools with no code: Google Workspace Flows / AppSheet Automation or an integration platform may be simpler.

**Cost:** No additional charge for consumer Google accounts or Workspace plans; usage is limited by Apps Script quotas (executions, runtime, URL fetch calls) which are lower on consumer accounts than on Workspace accounts. Check the official Apps Script quotas page for current limits.
